To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the accuracy of a Monte Carlo model of light transport for optical tomography is improved when (i) the photon delivery is accurately modeled, (ii) the photon collection is modeled with accurate acceptance angles, (iii) accurate anisotropy factors are employed, (iv) the phantom size is large compared to the transport mean free paths of the medium, and (v) the anisotropy factor is small.
Monte Carlo simulations validate and guide the development of the numerical RTE solver for small animal optical tomographic imaging.

the development of novel optical tomographic methods for the detection and characterization of small tumors in small animals, such as rodents.
the development of an optical tomographic system for imaging of small animals and tissue phantoms.

the development and application of a unique forward solver of the coupled RTEs to rapidly compute the time-dependent excitation, fluorescent, and scattered light propagation in small animals for small animal tomography.

the Monte Carlo simulations validate the forward model for the small animal tomography and guide the development of the forward model for deployment in small volume optical tomography.
Monte Carlo simulations of the coupled RTEs are an essential tool in the design and development of a fast RTE solver for small animal optical tomographic imaging.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a unique numerical forward model to solve the RTEs for rapidly computing time dependent excitation and fluorescent propagation in small animal optical imaging and tomography.
we developed a novel RTE solver for time-dependent transport limited propagation in small animal optical imaging and validated this RTE solver using Monte Carlo simulations.

the Monte Carlo simulations are a useful validation tool for the forward model of optical tomography, and that the forward model should be based upon the accurate anisotropic scattering factor and source models of photon propagation in order to best predict transport-limited measurements.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the accuracy of a forward solver for time-dependent, transport limited fluorescent boundary measurements in small animal optical imaging is dependent upon the anisotropic scattering properties of the tissue and the source model used to deliver photons to the tissue.
the accuracy of a forward model in small animal optical imaging depends not only on the accuracy of the anisotropic factors but also on the accuracy of source and acceptance models.
the Monte Carlo simulations can be used to validate and guide the development of an appropriate radiative transfer equation (RTE) solver for deployment in optical tomography.
